newsitem.title: FRANCE: French film director Marcel Carne dies.
newsitem.headline: French film director Marcel Carne dies.

text.p: French director Marcel Carne, who fathered a film legend with "Les Enfants du Paradis" in the 1940s, died on Thursday, a spokeswoman for the culture ministry said. He was 90.
Carne died before dawn at a hospital in Clamart near Paris.

He won widespread acclaim for classics "Quai des Brumes" and "Hotel du Nord" in the 1930s and 1940s. He will probably best be remembered for "Les Enfants du Paradis", which evoked the sleazy street life of Paris in the mid-19th century.
Although he worked consistently for three decades after World War Two, his later career was plagued by critical and commercial setbacks and he never recovered the success of his golden years.
President Jacques Chirac paid tribute to the director.
"It's rare that an artists sees his work become part of the culture of a whole people to such an extent," Chirac said in a message released by his office.
"Thank-you to Marcel Carne for making us dream so much," he said.
Actor Francois Perier, who worked alongside Carne, praised him for the way he treated his cast.
"Once he trusted you, he would give you free rein. He didn't burden you with ideas that some directors suddenly think up. He would talk to people for a long time before starting a film," Perier said.
Despite his age, Carne proved his stamina at the 1992 Cannes film festival, partying until the early hours every night.
Born in Paris in 1906, Carne chose not to take up his father's trade as a carpenter. He quickly found a path into the emerging art of filmmaking.

Obsessed by the cinema early on, he took lessons in photography and became editor of Film-Hebdo magazine. He was later hired as an assistant to director Rene Clair and made his first full-length production, "Jenny", in 1936.
